FrMS88-de1560-d1e111.summary: Poses the second question: whether the subject of the first complex principle, said of God and creature, has the same concept. The opening negative argument cites Dionysius (De divinis nominibus): of God there is neither word nor name.
claims: Dionysius seems to deny that any name or concept applies to God.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e124.summary: Gives the contrary from Dionysius (De div. nom. 2): divine names are attributed to creatures. Then begins four preambles, the first being that 'concept' here does not mean the act of understanding, for then there would be no difficulty.
claims: Divine names are attributed to creatures.
'Concept' in the question does not mean the act of understanding.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e135.summary: Second preamble: concept here is not a being of reason, since the question concerns an essential predicate, and neither God nor creature is quidditatively a being of reason; a quidditative concept is sought.
claims: The concept at issue is a quidditative concept, not a being of reason.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e144.summary: Third preamble: concept cannot fittingly mean the object in cognized being, since whatever is constituted from a real being and a being of reason is a being of reason; a concept of a real object as cognized would therefore be a being of reason.
claims: Whatever is composed of a real being and a being of reason is a being of reason.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e158.summary: Fourth preamble: concept here means the known quiddity or quidditative notion at which the act of intellect terminates. On these suppositions Meyronnes asserts that being, the subject of the first principle, has one concept univocal to God and creature, proving it through a rule of 'the Doctor' (Scotus): when an intellect is certain of one concept and doubtful about two, the concept of which it is certain is other than the two about which it doubts.
claims: 'Concept' means the known quiddity terminating the act of understanding.
Being has one concept univocal to God and creature.
An intellect certain of one concept and doubtful of two others has a concept distinct from them.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e178.summary: First clarification of the rule: every common name is either univocal or equivocal, since their definitions are by immediate contraries — there is no middle between having one formal notion and not having one.
claims: Every common name is either univocal or equivocal, with no middle.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e194.summary: Further support: the equivocal applies to its equivocates through multiple notions, the univocal through one notion.
claims: Equivocals apply by many notions, univocals by one.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e201.summary: Second clarification: the certain concept can only be conceived as inferior, equal, or superior to the doubtful concepts; it is neither inferior nor equal, so it is superior; every superior concept, as communicable, is univocal.
claims: The certain concept is superior to the doubtful concepts and hence univocal.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e214.summary: Third clarification: an intellect with one certain concept compossible with two others conceives it as communicable to them, and a communicable concept as such is univocal.
claims: A concept conceived as communicable to several is univocal.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e221.summary: Fourth clarification: an intellect having a concept indeterminate with respect to certain determinate concepts has a univocal concept with respect to them; the intellect certain of one and doubtful of two is such.
claims: An indeterminate concept relative to determinate ones is univocal to them.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e233.summary: Formulates the argument: many have been certain that God is a being while doubting whether he is first or not first, finite or infinite; hence the concept of being is univocal to these. Then raises four lines of objection, the first 'logical': the rule seems to conclude equally for equivocals, since one can be certain that 'a dog runs' while doubting which dog (the barking animal or another).
claims: Since one can be certain God is a being while doubting whether he is finite or infinite, being is a univocal concept.
Objection: the rule seems to hold equally of equivocal terms.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e259.summary: Second logical counterexample: one can be certain that health is present while doubting whether it is in urine or in an animal.
claims: Objection: certainty about an analogical term coexists with doubt about its bearer.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e266.summary: Physical objection: philosophers were certain that the soul informs the body and that the body is animated, yet doubted whether the soul is body or spirit, which have nothing in common.
claims: Objection: certainty about the soul coexisted with doubt between body and spirit, which share no univocal concept.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e275.summary: Further counterexample: philosophers were certain God is necessary being but doubted whether finite or infinite, yet necessary being is not univocal to finite and infinite.
claims: Objection: necessary being is not univocal to finite and infinite.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e282.summary: Metaphysical objection: philosophers were certain of the eternity of the world while doubting its finitude or infinity, yet eternity is not univocal to finite and infinite.
claims: Objection: eternity is not univocal to finite and infinite.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e291.summary: Further counterexample: philosophers were certain God is the first cause but doubted his finitude or infinity, yet first cause is not univocal to finite and infinite.
claims: Objection: first cause is not univocal to finite and infinite.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e299.summary: Theological objection: theologians agree the soul has powers but doubt whether they are substance or accident; and that divine persons are constituted by properties, while doubting whether absolute or relative — yet 'power' and 'property' are not univocal across these alternatives.
claims: Objection: 'power' and 'property' are not univocal to substance/accident or absolute/relative.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e315.summary: Transitional rubric introducing the replies to the objections.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e318.summary: Reply to the logical objections: with equivocals like 'dog' and 'health' there is certainty only about the word, not about any concept. The philosophers were certain not only of the word 'being' but of one concept corresponding to it; words are imposed by convention, while concepts are the same for all.
claims: Certainty about equivocals concerns only the word.
Concepts are the same for everyone, whereas words are conventional.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e331.summary: Reply about the soul: the philosophers were not certain of any specific concept, but only of a concept of soul common to all its candidates, which perhaps is a common univocal concept.
claims: The certain concept of soul was a common concept, perhaps univocal.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e340.summary: Reply about necessary being: the rule presupposes an essential order such that the certain concept remains certain while the others are doubtful, and it is impossible for it to be doubtful while the others are certain, and not conversely.
claims: The rule requires an essential, non-reversible order between the certain and the doubtful concepts.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e353.summary: Applies the refinement: necessary being is not so related to finite and infinite, since one can be certain of infinity and doubt necessity (as with the heavens); the same holds for eternity and infinity, and vice versa, which answers those instances.
claims: Necessary being and eternity do not satisfy the essential order required by the rule.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e365.summary: Reply to the theological objections: theologians are certain only of common concepts — 'power' as the concept of a productive principle, abstracted from absolute and relative, and likewise for properties. Then turns to others' solutions to the whole argument, first the reply that, granting the major, the concepts in the minor are not really distinct though they seem two.
claims: 'Power' and 'property' are common concepts abstracted from absolute and relative.
Reported reply: the seemingly distinct concepts are not really distinct.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e383.summary: Argues against that reply: natural philosophers proceeded demonstratively through this concept (of being).
claims: Natural philosophers demonstrated by means of the concept of being.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e388.summary: Further: contradictories cannot be verified of the same; so the same concept cannot be both certain and uncertain.
claims: One concept cannot be both certain and doubtful.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e395.summary: Reports another reply: the intellect is certain of a disjunctive and indeterminate concept, but doubtful about either determinate disjunct.
claims: Reported reply: certainty attaches to a disjunction, doubt to the determinate disjuncts.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e400.summary: Refutes that reply: on it philosophers would have been as certain that God is triune as that he is a being, since they were certain he is triune or not triune; likewise certain about the Incarnation. Since their certainty about being differs from this, being has one concept of which the intellect is certain.
claims: Certainty about mere disjunctions would make philosophers certain about the Trinity and Incarnation, which is absurd.
Being has one concept of which the intellect is certain.

FrMS88-de1560-d1e418.summary: Rejects the view that the concept of being is 'mixed', since the concept of being is simply simple. Answers the opening argument: there is no proper name or word for God, nor a concept, without there being something more common.
claims: The concept of being is simply simple and not mixed.
Dionysius denies a proper name of God, not a common concept.

FrMS88-de1560.summary: The second question of the prologue asks whether the subject of the first complex principle (being), said of God and creature, has one and the same concept. After four preambles fixing 'concept' as the known quiddity or quidditative notion terminating the intellect's act (not the act itself, nor a being of reason, nor the object in cognized being), Meyronnes affirms that being has one concept univocal to God and creature. His proof is Scotus' rule of the certain and doubtful concept: an intellect certain of one concept while doubtful of two others has a concept distinct from both, and that concept is univocal — a rule he justifies four ways (the immediate opposition of univocal and equivocal, the superiority of the certain concept, its communicability, its indeterminacy). Since philosophers were certain God is a being while doubting whether he is finite or infinite, first or not first, the concept of being is univocal. He answers logical, physical, metaphysical, and theological counterexamples (dog, health, soul as body or spirit, necessary being, eternity, first cause, powers of the soul, constitutive properties) by insisting that certainty about equivocals concerns only the word, by refining the rule to require an essential order of certainty, and by identifying genuinely common concepts in the counterexamples. He also rejects attempts to evade the argument by denying distinct concepts, by appealing to certainty about indeterminate disjunctions (which would make philosophers certain about the Trinity and Incarnation), or by positing a 'mixed' concept, since the concept of being is simply simple.
claims: 'Concept' in the question means the known quiddity terminating the act of intellect.
The concept of being is one and univocal to God and creatures.
An intellect certain of one concept and doubtful of two others has a distinct, univocal concept of which it is certain.
Certainty about an equivocal term concerns only the word, not any concept.
The concept of being is simply simple and cannot be a mixed concept.
